title: Neuropsych Testing Cost by State: Billed Rates vs Medicare
description: Published state-by-state Medicare figures for the first hour of neuropsychological testing evaluation, including how many clinicians bill it in each state.
main_html:
What is the answer?

What a neuropsychological evaluation is billed at varies a lot by state. What Medicare allows for it barely varies at all.

First hour of neuropsychological testing evaluation, by state: what should you know?

Code 96132, office setting, calendar year 2024 Medicare claims.

Illinois$351.34$127.22241

Georgia$280.58$121.25193

Ohio$320.99$118.07153
Michigan$314.48$119.09169
Massachusetts$304.26$130.62185

Nationally the code was billed at $317.32 and allowed at $124.09, across 6,086 clinicians.

What the clinician count tells you: what should you know?

The right-hand column is supply. A state with few billing clinicians is usually a state with a long wait, not a bargain.

Counts are Medicare-billing clinicians only. Practices that decline insurance are invisible here, and in some metros they are a large share of capacity.

Reading a state figure honestly: what should you know?

These are averages across a whole state. A large metro and a rural county sit inside the same number.

CMS hides any cell covering fewer than 11 patients, so smaller states may show as not published. We leave those blank rather than filling them.

Questions to ask a local practice: what should you know?

  • What is the wait for an evaluation appointment?
  • Do you bill insurance, or are you self-pay only?
  • What is your rate for the first evaluation hour?
  • How many total hours do you typically bill?

Common mistake: choosing a state figure over a local quote. The figure is context; the quote is the price.

How can you compare a local quote with the state row?

Start a worksheet with the state name, the billing code, the office setting and the claims year shown above. Copy both column labels along with their values. A number without its label is easy to mistake for a complete evaluation price. The table describes the first evaluation hour under one code; it does not describe every service your practice may propose.

Next, leave a separate column for the practice's written estimate. Ask the billing office to identify the services included in that estimate, the units of each service and any separate report or feedback charges. Do not multiply the first-hour figure by every hour on the appointment calendar: ask which code and unit the practice actually plans to bill for each part. Keep unanswered items marked as unknown rather than silently treating them as included.

If two practices give different totals, compare their scope before comparing their prices. One quote may include record review and a feedback appointment while another lists those separately. Write down whether the amount is a cash quote, a submitted insurance charge or an estimate of your own payment. Those are different questions, and the state table cannot resolve them for a particular insurance plan.

What should you do when your location is not represented?

The selected state rows are examples from the published dataset, not a directory of every local option. A missing state or practice is not evidence that testing is unavailable there. Likewise, a clinician count in this table cannot tell you whether an office is accepting new patients, sees your age group or answers your referral question. Confirm those details directly before using price to narrow your choices.

For a comparison across state lines, add travel, repeat visits and the report deadline to your worksheet without assigning invented amounts. Ask each office which visits require attendance and how results are delivered. Keep the original written quotes and the date each office confirmed them. Use this page to understand what a published figure measures; use the practice's answers to decide whether the proposed evaluation fits the question you need answered.

Where these numbers come from, and what they are not: what should you know?

Method: we pull the published rows for each billing code, keep the average submitted charge and the average Medicare allowed amount, and print them unchanged. Nothing is modelled, averaged across codes, or adjusted.

  • The submitted charge is what clinicians billed. It is list price. Almost nobody pays it.
  • The allowed amount is what Medicare permitted, including the patient's coinsurance. It is a negotiated price.
  • These are Medicare fee-for-service claims. The patients skew 65 and older.
  • If you are paying cash or using commercial insurance, neither figure is your price. Use the gap between them as a bargaining range, not a quote.
  • CMS hides any cell covering fewer than 11 patients, so some states are missing. We print "not published" there rather than guessing.

Common mistake: reading the allowed amount as "the real price" and expecting a clinic to match it. It is what one payer pays one set of clinicians.

What to do next: what should you know?

Use the state row as a sanity check on the first quote you receive, then get a second quote locally.

Educational only. Not medical advice. No endorsements or rankings.

search_strengthening.definition: Neuropsych testing cost is what a practice bills for a neuropsychological evaluation: the clinical interview, the hours of test administration and scoring, and the written report with a feedback session. By state, the billed rate moves with local market prices while the Medicare-allowed amount barely moves, so a cash payer should start from the billed figure for their own state.

faq.q: How much does neuropsych testing cost in my state?
faq.a: Start from the billed first-hour figure for your state on this page, then multiply by the hours the practice quotes for testing, scoring and the report. Ask the practice for its own written estimate, because the state figure is a starting point, not a quote.

faq.q: Why is the Medicare amount so different from the billed amount?
faq.a: Medicare sets one allowed amount nationally with a small geographic adjustment, while billed charges are each practice's list price. Insurance usually pays close to its allowed amount; a cash payer is quoted something nearer the billed amount.

faq.q: What should I ask a practice before booking testing?
faq.a: Ask how many hours of testing and scoring they expect, whether the report and feedback session are included, whether they bill insurance or are out of network, and what a cash or self-pay rate would be.
